entries.f8c56c8063f312ed200c4dae2c83ac7556c0a1a5: <div sID="gen17624" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Jer.19" sID="Jer.19"/> <div eID="gen17624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17626" type="x-p"/> The same melancholy theme is the subject of this chapter that was of those foregoing—the approaching ruin of Judah and Jerusalem for their sins. This Jeremiah had often foretold; here he has particularly full orders to foretel it again. I. He must set their sins in order before them, as he had often done, especially their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4-Jer.19.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. He must describe the particular judgments which were now coming apace upon them for these sins, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.6-Jer.19.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. III. He must do this in the valley of Tophet, with great solemnity, and for some particular reasons, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.2-Jer.19.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. IV. He must summon a company of the elders together to be witnesses of this, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1">ver. 1</reference>. V. He must confirm this, and endeavour to affect his hearers with it, by a sign, which was the breaking of an earthen bottle, signifying that they should be dashed to pieces like a potter's vessel, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.10-Jer.19.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. VI. When he had done this in the valley of Tophet he ratified it in the court of the temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.14-Jer.19.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. Thus were all likely means tried to awaken this stupid senseless people to repentance, that their ruin might be prevented; but all in vain.
entries.fe5507f4a8ab0b06ded5005df0f2177896edbc1d: <div eID="gen17626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17625" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen17627" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Go and get a potter's earthen bottle, and <hi type="italic">take</hi> of the ancients of the people, and of the ancients of the priests; <hi type="super">2</hi> And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee, <hi type="super">3</hi> And say, Hear ye the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O kings of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem; Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth, his ears shall tingle. <hi type="super">4</hi> Because they have forsaken me, and have estranged this place, and have burned incense in it unto other gods, whom neither they nor their fathers have known, nor the kings of Judah, and have filled this place with the blood of innocents; <hi type="super">5</hi> They have built also the high places of Baal, to burn their sons with fire <hi type="italic">for</hi> burnt offerings unto Baal, which I commanded not, nor spake <hi type="italic">it,</hi> neither came <hi type="italic">it</hi> into my mind: <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of slaughter. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place; and I will cause them to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hands of them that seek their lives: and their carcases will I give to be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will make this city desolate, and a hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and they shall eat every one the flesh of his friend in the siege and straitness, wherewith their enemies, and they that seek their lives, shall straiten them. <div eID="gen17627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17628" type="x-p"/> The corruption of man having made it necessary that <hi type="italic">precept</hi> should be <hi type="italic">upon precept, and line upon line</hi> (so unapt are we to receive, and so very apt to let slip, the things of God), the grace of God has provided that there shall be, accordingly, <hi type="italic">precept upon precept, and line upon line,</hi> that those who are irreclaimable may be inexcusable. For this reason the prophet is here sent with a message to the same purport with what he had often delivered, but with some circumstances that might make it the more taken notice of, a thing which ministers should study, for a little circumstance may sometimes be a great advantage, and those that would win souls must be wise. <div eID="gen17628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17629" type="x-p"/> I. He must take of the elders and chief men, both in church and state, to be his auditors and witnesses to what he said—<hi type="italic">the ancients of the people and the ancients of the priests,</hi> the most eminent men both in the magistracy and in the ministry, that they might be <hi type="italic">faithful witnesses to record,</hi> as those <reference osisRef="Isa.8.2">Isa. viii. 2</reference>. It is strange that these great men should be at the beck of a poor prophet, and obey his summons to attend him out of the city, they know not whither and they knew not why. But, though the generality of the elders were disaffected to him, yet it is likely that there were some few among them who looked upon him as a prophet of the Lord, and would pay this respect to the heavenly vision. Note, Persons of rank and figure have an opportunity of honouring God, by a diligent attendance on the ministry of the word and other divine institutions; and they ought to think it an honour, and no disparagement to themselves, yea, though the circumstances be mean and despicable. It is certain that the greatest of men is less than the least of the ordinances of God. <div eID="gen17629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17630" type="x-p"/> II. He must <hi type="italic">go to the valley of the son of Hinnom,</hi> and deliver this message there; for <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord</hi> is not bound to any one place; as good a sermon may be preached in the valley of Tophet as in the gate of the temple. Christ preached on a mountain and out of a ship. This valley lay partly on the south side of Jerusalem, but the prophet's way to it was <hi type="italic">by the entry on the east gate—the sun gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.2">v. 2</reference>), so some render it, and suppose it to look not towards the sun-rising, but the noon sun—<hi type="italic">the potter's gate,</hi> so some. This sermon must be preached in that place, in <hi type="italic">the valley of the son of Hinnom,</hi> 1. Because there they had been guilty of the vilest of their idolatries, the sacrificing of their children to Moloch, a horrid piece of impiety, which the sight of the place might serve to remind them of and upbraid them with. 2. Because there they should feel the sorest of their calamities; there the greatest slaughter should be made among them; and, it being the common sink of the city, let them look upon it and see what a miserable spectacle this magnificent city would be when it should be all like the valley of Tophet. God bids him go thither, <hi type="italic">and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee,</hi> when thou comest thither; whereby it appears (as Mr. Gataker well observed) that God's messages were frequently not revealed to the prophets before the very instant of time wherein they were to deliver them. <div eID="gen17630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17631" type="x-p"/> III. He must give general notice of a general ruin now shortly coming upon Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.3">v. 3</reference>. He must, as those that make proclamation, begin with an <hi type="italic">Oyes: Hear you the word of the Lord,</hi> though it be a terrible word, for you may thank yourselves if it be so. Both rulers and ruled must attend to it, at their peril; the <hi type="italic">kings of Judah,</hi> the king and his sons, the king and his princes and privy-counsellors, must hear the word of the King of kings, for, high as they are, he is above them. The <hi type="italic">inhabitants of Jerusalem</hi> also must hear what God has to say to them. Both princes and people have contributed to the national guilt and must concur in the national repentance, or they will both share in the national ruin. Let them all know that <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> who is therefore able to do what he threatens, though he is <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> nay, because he is so, will therefore punish them in the first place for their iniquities (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">He will bring evil upon this place</hi> (upon <hi type="italic">Judah and Jerusalem</hi>) so surprising, and so dreadful, that <hi type="italic">whosoever hears</hi> it, <hi type="italic">his ears shall tingle;</hi> whosoever hears the prediction of it, hears the report and representation of it, it shall make such an impression of terror upon him that he shall still think he hears it sounding in his ears and shall not be able to get it out of his mind. The ruin of Eli's house is thus described (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.11">1 Sam. iii. 11</reference>), and of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.12">2 Kings xxi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen17631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17632" type="x-p"/> IV. He must plainly tell them what their sins were for which God had this controversy with them, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4-Jer.19.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. They are charged with apostasy from God (<hi type="italic">They have forsaken me</hi>) and abuse of the privileges of the visible church, and which they had been dignified—<hi type="italic">They have estranged this place.</hi> Jerusalem (the holy city), the temple (the holy house), which was designed for the honour of God and the support of his kingdom among men, they had alienated from those purposes, and (as some render the word) <hi type="italic">they had strangely abused.</hi> They had so polluted both with their wickedness that God had disowned both, and abandoned them to ruin. He charges them with an affection for and the adoration of false <hi type="italic">gods,</hi> such as <hi type="italic">neither they nor their fathers have known,</hi> such as never had recommended themselves to their belief and esteem by any acts of power or goodness done for them or their ancestors, as that God had abundantly done whom they forsook; yet they took them at a venture for their gods; nay, being fond of change and novelty, they liked them the better for their being upstarts, and new fashions in religion were as grateful to their fancies as in other things. They also stand charged with murder, wilful murder, from malice prepense: <hi type="italic">They have filled this place with the blood of innocents.</hi> It was Manasseh's sin (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">which the Lord would not pardon.</hi> Nay, as if idolatry and murder, committed separately, were not bad enough and affront enough to God and man, they have put them together, have consolidated them into one complicated crime, that of burning their children in the fire to Baal (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">v. 5</reference>), which was the most insolent defiance to all the laws both of natural and revealed religion that ever mankind was guilty of; and by it they openly declared that they loved their new gods better than ever they loved the true God, though they were such cruel task-masters that they required human sacrifices (inhuman I should call them), which the Lord Jehovah, whose all lives and souls are, never demanded from his worshippers; he never <hi type="italic">spoke</hi> of such a thing, nor <hi type="italic">came it into his mind.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">ch. vii. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen17632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17633" type="x-p"/> V. He must endeavour to affect them with the greatness of the desolation that was coming upon them. He must tell them (as he had done before, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">ch. vii. 32</reference>) that this <hi type="italic">valley of the son of Hinnom</hi> shall acquire a new name, <hi type="italic">the valley of slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.6">v. 6</reference>), for (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">v. 7</reference>) multitudes shall <hi type="italic">fall</hi> there <hi type="italic">by the sword,</hi> when either they sally out upon the besiegers and are repulsed or attempt to make their escape and are seized: <hi type="italic">They</hi> shall <hi type="italic">fall before their enemies,</hi> who not only endeavour to make themselves masters of their houses and estates, but have such an implacable enmity to them that they <hi type="italic">seek their lives;</hi> they thirst after their blood, and, when they are dead, will not allow a cartel for the burying of the slain, but <hi type="italic">their carcases</hi> shall <hi type="italic">be meat for the fowls of the heaven and beasts of the earth.</hi> What a dismal place will the valley of Tophet be then! And as for those that remain within the city, and will not capitulate with the besiegers, they shall perish for want of food, when first they have eaten <hi type="italic">the flesh of their sons and daughters,</hi> and dearest <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> through the <hi type="italic">straitness wherewith their enemies shall straiten them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">v. 9</reference>. This was threatened in the law as an instance of the extremity to which the judgments of God should reduce them (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev. xxvi. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deut. xxviii. 53</reference>) and was accomplished, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">Lam. iv. 10</reference>. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> the whole <hi type="italic">city</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">desolate,</hi> the houses laid in ashes, the inhabitants slain or taken prisoners; there shall be no resort to it, nor any thing in it but what looks rueful and horrid; so that <hi type="italic">every one that passes by shall be astonished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.8">v. 8</reference>), as he had said before, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">ch. xviii. 16</reference>. That place which holiness had made <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth</hi> sin had made the reproach and shame of the whole earth. <div eID="gen17633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17634" type="x-p"/> VI. He must assure them that all their attempts to prevent and avoid this ruin, so long as they continued impenitent and unreformed, would be fruitless and vain (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem</hi> (of the princes and senators of Judah and Jerusalem) <hi type="italic">in this place,</hi> in the royal palace, which lay on the south side of the city, not far from the place where the prophet now stood. Note, There is no fleeing from God's justice but by fleeing to his mercy. Those that will not make good God's counsel, by humbling themselves under his mighty hand, shall find that God will make void their counsel and blast their projects, which they think ever so well concerted for their own preservation. There is <hi type="italic">no counsel</hi> or strength <hi type="italic">against the Lord.</hi>
entries.e7c7e349c84c24f5a02f48fb081c307c0513d1ba: <div eID="gen17634" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen17635" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Then shalt thou break the bottle in the sight of the men that go with thee, <hi type="super">11</hi> And shalt say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Even so will I break this people and this city, as <hi type="italic">one</hi> breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again: and they shall bury <hi type="italic">them</hi> in Tophet, till <hi type="italic">there be</hi> no place to bury. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thus will I do unto this place, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to the inhabitants thereof, and <hi type="italic">even</hi> make this city as Tophet: <hi type="super">13</hi> And the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses of the kings of Judah, shall be defiled as the place of Tophet, because of all the houses upon whose roofs they have burned incense unto all the host of heaven, and have poured out drink offerings unto other gods. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then came Jeremiah from Tophet, whither the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had sent him to prophesy; and he stood in the court of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house; and said to all the people, <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring upon this city and upon all her towns all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they have hardened their necks, that they might not hear my words. <div eID="gen17635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17636" type="x-p"/> The message of wrath delivered in the <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.9">foregoing verses</reference> is here enforced, that it might gain credit, two ways:— <div eID="gen17636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17637" type="x-p"/> I. By a visible sign. The prophet was to take along with him an <hi type="italic">earthen bottle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.1">v. 1</reference>), and, when he had delivered his message, he was to <hi type="italic">break the bottle</hi> to pieces (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.10">v. 10</reference>), and the same that were auditors of the sermon must be spectators of the sign. He had compared this people, in the chapter before, to the potter's clay, which is easily marred in the making. But some might say, "It is past that with us; we have been made and hardened long since." "And what though you be," says he, "the potter's vessel is as soon broken in the hand of any man as the vessel while it is soft clay is marred in the potter's hand, and its case is, in this respect, much worse, that the vessel while it is soft clay, though it be marred, may be moulded again, but, after it is hardened, when it is broken it can never be pieced again." Perhaps what they see will affect them more than what they only hear talk of; that is the intention of sacramental signs, and teaching by symbols was anciently used. In the explication of this sign he must inculcate what he had before said, with a further reference to the place where this was done, in the valley of Tophet. 1. As the bottle was easily, irresistibly, and irrecoverably broken by the Chaldean army, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.11">v. 11</reference>. They depended much upon the firmness of their constitution, and the fixedness of their courage, which they thought hardened them like a vessel of brass; but the prophet shows that all that did but harden them like a vessel of earth, which, though hard, is brittle and sooner broken than that which is not so hard. Though they were made vessels of honour, still they were vessels of earth, and so they shall be made to know if they dishonour God and themselves, and serve not the purposes for which they were made. It is God himself, who made them, that resolves to unmake them: <hi type="italic">I will break this people and this city,</hi> dash them in pieces like <hi type="italic">a potter's vessel;</hi> the doom of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Ps. ii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Rev. ii. 27</reference>), but now Jerusalem's doom, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.14">Isa. xxx. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">A potter's vessel,</hi> when once broken, <hi type="italic">cannot be made whole again, cannot be cured,</hi> so the word is. The ruin of Jerusalem shall be an utter ruin; no hand can repair it but his that broke it; and if they return to him, though he has torn, he will heal. 2. This was done in Tophet, to signify two things:—(1.) That Tophet should be the receptacle of the slain: <hi type="italic">They shall bury in Tophet till there be no place to bury</hi> any more there; they shall jostle for room to lay their dead, and a very little room will then serve those who, while they lived, <hi type="italic">laid house to house and field to field.</hi> Those that would be <hi type="italic">placed alone in the midst of the earth</hi> while they were above ground, and obliged all about them to keep their distance, must lie with the multitude when they are underground, for there are innumerable before them. (2.) That Tophet should be a resemblance of the whole city (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make this city as Tophet.</hi> As they had filled the valley of Tophet with the slain which they sacrificed to their idols, so God will fill the whole city with the slain that shall fall as sacrifices to the justice of God. We read (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2 Kings xxiii. 10</reference>) of Josiah's defiling Tophet, because it had been abused to idolatry, which he did (as should seem, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.14">v. 14</reference>) by <hi type="italic">filling it with the bones of men;</hi> and, whatever it was before, thenceforward it was looked upon as a detestable place. Dead carcases, and other filth of the city, were carried thither, and a fire was continually kept there for the burning of it. This was the posture of that valley when Jeremiah was sent thither to prophesy; and so execrable a place was it looked upon to be that, in the language of our Saviour's time, hell was called, in allusion to it, <hi type="italic">Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom.</hi> "Now" (says God) "since that blessed reformation, when Tophet was defiled, did not proceed as it ought to have done, nor prove a thorough reformation, but though the idols in Tophet were abolished and made odious those in Jerusalem remained, therefore will I do with the city as Josiah did by Tophet, fill it with the bodies of men, and make it a heap of rubbish." Even <hi type="italic">the houses of Jerusalem, and</hi> those <hi type="italic">of the kings of Judah,</hi> the royal palaces not excepted, <hi type="italic">shall be defiled as the place of Tophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">v. 13</reference>), and for the same reason, because of the idolatries that have been committed there; since they will not defile them by a reformation, God will defile them by a destruction, <hi type="italic">because</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">roofs of their houses they have burnt incense unto the host of heaven.</hi> The flat roofs of their houses were sometimes used by devout people as convenient places for prayer (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.9">Acts x. 9</reference>), and by idolaters they were used as high places, on which they sacrificed to strange gods, especially to <hi type="italic">the host of heaven,</hi> the sun, moon, and stars, that there they might be so much nearer to them and have a clearer and fuller view of them. We read of those that <hi type="italic">worshipped the host of heaven upon the house-tops</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zeph. i. 5</reference>), and of <hi type="italic">altars on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings xxiii. 12</reference>. This sin upon the house-tops brought a curse into the house, which consumed it, and made it a dunghill like Tophet. <div eID="gen17637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17638" type="x-p"/> II. By a solemn recognition and ratification of what he had said <hi type="italic">in the court of the Lord's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.14-Jer.19.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. The prophet returned from Tophet to the temple, which stood upon the hill over that valley, and there confirmed, and probably repeated, what he had said in the valley of Tophet, for the benefit of those who had not heard it; what he had said he would stand to. Here, as often before, he both assures them of judgments coming upon them and assigns the cause of them, which was their sin. Both these are here put together in a little compass, with a reference to all that had gone before. 1. The accomplishment of the prophecies is here the judgment threatened. The people flattered themselves with a conceit that God would be better than his word, that the threatening was but to frighten them and keep them in awe a little; but the prophet tells them that they deceive themselves if they think so: <hi type="italic">For thus saith the Lord of hosts,</hi> who is able to make his words good, <hi type="italic">I will bring upon this city, and upon all her towns,</hi> all the smaller cities that belong to Jerusalem the metropolis, <hi type="italic">all the evil that I have pronounced against it.</hi> Note, Whatever men may think to the contrary, the executions of Providence will fully answer the predictions of the word, and God will appear as terrible against sin and sinners as the scripture makes him; nor shall the unbelief of men make either his promises or his threatenings of no effect or of less effect than they were thought to be of. 2. The contempt of the prophecies is here the sin charged upon them, as the procuring cause of this judgment. It is <hi type="italic">because they have hardened their necks,</hi> and would not bow and bend them to the yoke of God's commands, would <hi type="italic">not hear my words,</hi> that is, would not heed them and yield obedience to them. Note, The obstinacy of sinners in their sinful ways is altogether their own fault; if their necks are hardened, it is their own act and deed, they have hardened them; if they are deaf to the word of God, it is because they have stopped their own ears. We have need therefore to pray that God, by his grace, would deliver us <hi type="italic">from hardness of heart and contempt of his word and commandments.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jer.19"/> <div eID="gen17638" type="x-p"/>

entries.116c5e7e43a31c487c89c1e17609295e06c601a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10008"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 19:1-15</reference>. The Desolation of the Jews for Their Sins Foretold in the Valley of Hinnom; the Symbol of Breaking a Bottle.</title> <div sID="gen17824" type="x-p"/> Referred by Maurer, &c., to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign.<div eID="gen17824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10008"/><hi type="bold">1. bottle--</hi>Hebrew, bakuk, so called from the gurgling sound which it makes when being emptied.<div eID="gen17825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancients--</hi>elders. As witnesses of the symbolic action (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.10">Jr 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Is 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">2</reference>), that the Jews might not afterwards plead ignorance of the prophecy. The seventy-two elders, composing the Sanhedrim, or Great Council, were taken partly from "the priests," partly from the other tribes, that is, "the people," the former presiding over spiritual matters, the latter over civil; the seventy-two represented the whole people. <div eID="gen17826" type="x-p"/>
entries.2db26259dfd2b993bb115624c680029f1e90a0e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10009"/><div sID="gen17827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10009"/><hi type="bold">2. valley of the son of Hinnom--</hi>or Tophet, south of Jerusalem, where human victims were offered, and children made to pass through the fire, in honor of Molech.<div eID="gen17827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east gate--</hi>Margin, "sun gate," sunrise being in the east. Maurer translates, the "potter's gate." Through it lay the road to the valley of Hinnom (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.8">Jos 15:8</reference>). The potters there formed vessels for the use of the temple, which was close by (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.19.10">Jr 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.2">Jr 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">Zec 11:13</reference>). The same as "the water gate toward the east" (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.26">Ne 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.37">12:37</reference>); so called from the brook Kedron. Calvin translates, as English Version and Margin. "It was monstrous perversity to tread the law under foot in so conspicuous a place, over which the sun daily rising reminded them of the light of God's law." <div eID="gen17828" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ee75140f82f162c230a986755c41635ed0e3540: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10010"/><div sID="gen17829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10010"/>3. The scene of their guilt is chosen as the scene of the denunciation against them.<div eID="gen17829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kings--</hi>the king and queen (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">Jr 13:18</reference>); or including the king's counsellors and governors under him.<div eID="gen17830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tingle--</hi>as if struck by a thunder peal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.11">1Sa 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.12">2Ki 21:12</reference>). <div eID="gen17831" type="x-p"/>
entries.2bf55b47d71ad6d3a864d4086fefff41e8a521ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10011"/><div sID="gen17832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10011"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Is 65:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">estranged this place--</hi>devoted it to the worship of strange gods: alienating a portion of the sacred city from God, the rightful Lord of the temple, city, and whole land.<div eID="gen17833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor their fathers--</hi>namely, the godly among them; their ungodly fathers God makes no account of.<div eID="gen17834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood of innocents--</hi>slain in honor of Molech (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jr 7:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.37">Psa 106:37</reference>). <div eID="gen17835" type="x-p"/>
entries.06bbd84398ed5a547fc0cdf45bc68d2dd8f67f5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10012"/><div sID="gen17836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10012"/><hi type="bold">5. commanded not--</hi>nay, more, I commanded the opposite (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Le 18:21</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">Jr 7:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">32</reference>). <div eID="gen17836" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1882c112768d82255cdc579a497e7c38088466e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10013"/><div sID="gen17837" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10013"/><hi type="bold">6. no more ... Tophet--</hi>from Hebrew, toph, "drum"; for in sacrificing children to Molech drums were beaten to drown their cries. Thus the name indicated the joy of the people at the fancied propitiation of the god by this sacrifice; in antithesis to its joyless name subsequently.<div eID="gen17837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">valley of slaughter--</hi>It should be the scene of slaughter, no longer of children, but of men; not of "innocents" (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jr 19:4</reference>), but of those who richly deserved their fate. The city could not be assailed without first occupying the valley of Hinnom, in which was the only fountain: hence arose the violent battle there. <div eID="gen17838" type="x-p"/>
entries.40ec09b268b37f170dfbfde8a4c42150eb130776: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10014"/><div sID="gen17839" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10014"/><hi type="bold">7. make void the counsel--</hi>defeat their plans for repelling the enemy (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1-2Chr.32.4">2Ch 32:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Is 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">22:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">11</reference>). Or their schemes of getting help by having recourse to idols [Calvin].<div eID="gen17839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in this place--</hi>The valley of Hinnom was to be the place of the Chaldean encampment; the very place where they looked for help from idols was to be the scene of their own slaughter. <div eID="gen17840" type="x-p"/>
entries.b174c8ca21788710fb894af4e5fdb1a0d2bb0802: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10015"/><div sID="gen17841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10015"/>8. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jr 18:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17841" type="x-p"/>
entries.0836881a75ec1911aee1e03ce5ba38ce3f7a4295: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10016"/><div sID="gen17842" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10016"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">De 28:53</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">La 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17842" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8e1473253142836df787814035e8dd0d4946445: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10017"/><div sID="gen17843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10017"/><hi type="bold">10. break ... bottle--</hi>a symbolical action, explained in <reference osisRef="Jer.19.11">Jr 19:11</reference>.<div eID="gen17843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17844" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the men--</hi>the elders of the people and of the priests (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.1">Jr 19:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.63">Jr 51:63</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.64">64</reference>). <div eID="gen17844" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f2d7dc902c1db9e3152b353f3fd78f12513c034: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10018"/><div sID="gen17845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10018"/><hi type="bold">11. as one breaketh a potter's vessel--</hi>expressing God's absolute sovereignty (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jr 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.14">Is 30:14</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">La 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen17845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot be made whole again--</hi>A broken potter's vessel cannot be restored, but a new one may be made of the same material. So God raised a new Jewish seed, not identical with the destroyed rebels, but by substituting another generation in their stead [Grotius].<div eID="gen17846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no place to bury--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.7.32">Jr 7:32</reference>). <div eID="gen17847" type="x-p"/>
entries.edac48e8d6b78dfc1d81167a0026e48869bdfbcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10019"/><div sID="gen17848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10019"/><hi type="bold">12. make this city as Tophet--</hi>that is, as defiled with dead bodies as Tophet. <div eID="gen17848" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2ed0445d562d8be4b0ccf1e82f7f0abec2e010e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10020"/><div sID="gen17849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10020"/><hi type="bold">13. shall be defiled--</hi>with dead bodies (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.12">Jr 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Ki 23:10</reference>).<div eID="gen17849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of all the houses--</hi>Rather, (explanatory of the previous "the houses ... and ... houses"), "even all the houses," &c. [Calvin].<div eID="gen17850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roofs--</hi>being flat, they were used as high places for sacrifices to the sun and planets (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">Jr 32:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zep 1:5</reference>). The Nabateans, south and east of the Dead Sea, a nation most friendly to the Jews, according to Strabo, had the same usage. <div eID="gen17851" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eb1d314e752cdec80974d25f1485f34f5d5e7d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10021"/><div sID="gen17852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10021"/><hi type="bold">14. court of the Lord's house--</hi>near Tophet; the largest court, under the open air, where was the greatest crowd (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.5">2Ch 20:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17852" type="x-p"/>
entries.1da1a0410fb44bf09b1b0fbe58ac3dd7092b04b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10022"/><div sID="gen17853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10022"/><hi type="bold">15. her towns--</hi>the suburban villages and towns near Jerusalem, such as Bethany. <chapter eID="Jer.19"/>

entries.3396d8df2a96e591f975ea3399fcfa89bd862000: <div eID="gen29778" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29779" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29780" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29780" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29779" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29781" type="x-p"/> By the significant type of breaking a potter's vessel, Jeremiah is directed to predict the utter desolation of Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.15">Jer 19:1-15</reference>. The prophets taught frequently by symbolic actions as well as by words. <div eID="gen29781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29782" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29783" type="x-p"/> Go and get a potter's earthen bottle - This discourse was also delivered some time in the reign of Jehoiakim. Under the type of breaking a potter's earthen bottle or jug, Jeremiah shows his enemies that the word of the Lord should stand, that Jerusalem should be taken and sacked, and they all carried into captivity. <div eID="gen29783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29784" type="x-p"/> Ancients of the priests - The chiefs of the twenty-four classes which David had established. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.4">1Chr 24:4</reference>.
entries.8ef684c4cf108a5ea0f9f103981f08f0edfac6d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29785" type="x-p"/> Estranged this place - Ye have devoted my temple to a widely different purpose from that for which it was erected.
entries.b491fd5837046c9251f6709d0c2debf1d0116617: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29786" type="x-p"/> Offerings unto Baal - A general name for all the popular idols; Baal, Moloch, Ashtaroth, etc.
entries.fc9d98394c35488c3bdc92c71e44b737bab91f30: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29787" type="x-p"/> I will make void the counsel of Judah - Probably this refers to some determination made to proclaim themselves independent, and pay no more tribute to the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen29787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29788" type="x-p"/> To be meat for the fowls - See on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">Jer 7:33</reference> (note).
entries.9d09e54d450b86e5ab94e2ea4be47a84e26cd2d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29789" type="x-p"/> I will cause them to eat the flesh of their sons - This was literally fulfilled when Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans. This also the prophet might have had in view.
entries.4c8ceab90e166b190c3f42f2f94a0eaf1c8d5082: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29790" type="x-p"/> Even so will I break this people and this city - The breaking of the bottle was the symbolical representation of the destruction of the city and of the state. <div eID="gen29790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29791" type="x-p"/> That cannot be made whole again - This seems to refer rather to the final destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, than to what was done by the Chaldeans. Jerusalem was healed after 70 years: but nearly 1800 years have elapsed since Jerusalem was taken and destroyed by the Romans; and it was then so broken, that it could not be made whole again.
entries.70cbd521e4b62a4d6bfb3b8a21616e5aac197f36: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29792" type="x-p"/> And even make this city as Tophet - A place of slaughter and destruction.
entries.71802f9d3f21ec23c25ce8c2ecf2f5e53f004169: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29793" type="x-p"/> Then came Jeremiah from Tophet - He had probably gone to the valley of Hinnom, and there repeated the discourse which he had a little before delivered to the chief priests and elders.
entries.246e9e3971e1474a215cce2287a060ecaa61420a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29794" type="x-p"/> Because they have hardened their necks - A metaphor taken from unruly and unbroken oxen, who resist the yoke, break and run away with their gears. So this people had broken and destroyed the yoke of the law.  <chapter eID="Jer.19"/> <div eID="gen29794" type="x-p"/>

entries.39de18d415d74a2a5c02c57baee7337025b1d77d: <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.13">Jer 19:1-13</reference> <div eID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> The Broken Pitcher.<hi type="italic">-</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1">Jer 19:1</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Thus said Jahveh: Go and buy a potter’s vessel, and take of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.2">Jer 19:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. And go forth into the valley of Benhinnom, which is before the gate Harsuth, and proclaim there the words which I shall speak unto thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.3">Jer 19:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. And say: Hear the word of Jahveh, ye kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: Thus hath said Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth his ears shall tingle.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jer 19:4</reference> <hi type="italic">. Because they have forsaken me, and disowned this place, and burnt incense in it to other gods whom they knew not, they, and their fathers, and the kings of Judah, and have filled this place with the blood of innocents,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jer 19:5</reference> <hi type="italic">. And have built high places for Baal, to burn their sons in the fire as burnt-offerings to Baal, which I have neither commanded nor spoken, nor came it into my heart.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.6">Jer 19:6</reference> <hi type="italic">. Therefore, behold, days come, saith Jahve, that this place shall no longer be called Tophet and Valley of Benhinnom, but Valley of Slaughter.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">Jer 19:7</reference> <hi type="italic">. And I make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and cause them to fall by the sword before their enemies and by the hand of them that seek their lives, and give their carcases to be food for the fowls of the heaven and the beast of the earth.</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.8">Jer 19:8</reference> <hi type="italic">. And make this city a dismay and a scoffing; every one that passeth thereby shall be dismayed and hiss because of all her strokes;</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer 19:9</reference> <hi type="italic">. And make them eat the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and each shall eat his neighbour’s flesh in the siege and straitness wherewith their enemies and they that seek after their lives shall straiten them. -</hi> Jer 19:10. <hi type="italic">And break the pitcher before the eyes of the men that go with thee,</hi> Jer 19:11. <hi type="italic">And say to them: Thus hath Jahve of hosts said: Even so will I break this people and this city as one breaketh this potter’s vessel, that it cannot be made whole again; and in Tophet shall they bury them, because there is no room to bury.</hi> Jer 19:12. <hi type="italic">Thus will I do unto this place, saith Jahveh, and its inhabitants, to make this city as Tophet.</hi> Jer 19:13. <hi type="italic">And the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah shall become, as the place Tophet, unclean, all the houses upon whose roofs they have burnt incense to the whole host of heaven and poured out drink-offerings to other gods."</hi> <div eID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> The purpose for which Jeremiah was to buy the earthen jar is told in <reference osisRef="Jer.19.10">Jer 19:10</reference>, and the meaning of breaking it in the valley of Benhinnom is shown in <reference osisRef="Jer.19.11">Jer 19:11</reference>-13. בּקבּק, from בּקק, to pour out, is a jar with a narrow neck, so called from the sound heard when liquid is poured out of it, although the vessel was used for storing honey, 1Ki 14:3. The appellation יוצר, former of earthen vessels, i.e., potter, is given to denote the jar as one which, on being broken, would shiver into many fragments. Before "of the elders of the people" a verb seems to be awanting, for which cause many supply ולקחתּ (according to <reference osisRef="Jer.41.12">Jer 41:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.10">Jer 43:10</reference>, etc.), rightly so far as sense is concerned; but we are hardly entitled to assume a lacuna in the text. That assumption is opposed by the ו before מזּקני; for we cannot straightway presume that this ו was put in after the verb had dropped out of the text. In that case the whole word would have been restored. We have here rather, as Schnur. saw, a bold <hi type="italic">constructio praegnans</hi>, the verb "buy" being also joined in zeugma with "of the elders:" buy a jar and (take) certain of the elders; cf. similar, only less bold, zeugmatic constr. in <reference osisRef="Job.4.10">Job 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.12">Job 10:12</reference>; Isa 58:5. "Elders of the priests," as in 2Ki 19:2, probably identical with the "princes (שׂרי) of the priests," <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.14">2Ch 36:14</reference>, are doubtless virtually the same as the "heads (ראשׁי) of the priests," <reference osisRef="Neh.12.7">Neh 12:7</reference>, the priests highest in esteem, not merely for their age, but also in virtue of their rank; just as the "elders of the people" were a permanent representation of the people, consisting of the heads of tribes, houses or septs, and families; cf. 1Ki 8:1-3, and my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. S. 218. Jeremiah was to take elders of the people and of the priesthood, because it was most readily to be expected of them that the word of God to be proclaimed would find a hearing amongst them. As to the valley of Benhinnom, see on Jer 7:31. שׁער החרסוּת, not Sun-gate (after חרס, <reference osisRef="Job.9.7">Job 9:7</reference>; Jdg 8:13), but Pottery or Sherd-gate, from חרס = חרשׂ, in rabbin. חרסית, potter’s clay. The <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. חרסוּת is the ancient form, not the modern (Hitz.), for the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is adapted to the rabbinical form. The clause, "which is before the <hi type="italic">Harsuth-gate</hi>," is not meant to describe more particularly the locality, sufficiently well known in Jerusalem, but has reference to the act to be performed there. The name, gate of חרסוּת, which nowhere else occurs, points no doubt to the breaking to shivers of the jar. Hence we are rather to translate Sherd-gate than Pottery-gate, the name having probably arisen amongst the people from the broken fragments which lay about this gate. Comm. are not at one as to which of the known city gates is meant. Hitz. and Kimchi are wrong in thinking of a gate of the court of the temple - the southern one. The context demands one of the city gates, two of which led into the Benhinnom valley: the Spring-or Fountain-gate at the south-east corner, and the Dung-gate on the south-west side of Zion; see on <reference osisRef="Neh.3.13">Neh 3:13</reference>-15. One of these two must be meant, but which of them it cannot be decided. there Jeremiah is to cry aloud the words which follow, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.3-Jer.19.8">Jer 19:3-8</reference>, and which bear on the kings of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. "Kings" in the plural, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">Jer 13:13</reference>, because the matter concerned not the reigning king only, but his successors too, who had been guilty of the sins to be punished.
entries.354e965a7357e5c53614cdc63818408a3ea87898: <reference osisRef="Jer.19.14-Jer.19.15">Jer 19:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> The Prophet Jeremiah and the Temple-Warden Pashur. - Jer 19:14. When Jeremiah, having performed the divine command, returned from Tophet to the city, he went into the court of the house of God and spoke to the people assembled there, v. 15: "Thus hath said Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I bring upon this city, and all its cities, all the evil that I have pronounced against it, because they stiffened their necks not to hear my words." "All the people" is the people present in the court of the temple as distinguished from the men who had accompanied Jeremiah into the valley of Benhinnom (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.10">Jer 19:10</reference>). מבי, the א having dropped off, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.16">Jer 39:16</reference>; 1Ki 21:21, 1Ki 21:29; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.2">2Sa 5:2</reference>, and often. "All its cities" are the towns that belonged to Jerusalem, were subject to it (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.1">Jer 34:1</reference>); in other words, the cities of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.15">Jer 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jer 9:10</reference>, etc. All the evil that I have pronounced against it, not merely in the valley of Benhinnom (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.3-Jer.19.13">Jer 19:3-13</reference>), but generally up till this time, by the mouth of Jeremiah. If we limit the reference of this view to the prophecy in Tophet, we must assume, with Näg., that Jeremiah repeated the substance of it here; and besides, that prophecy is not in keeping with "all its cities," inasmuch as it (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.3-Jer.19.13">Jer 19:3-13</reference>) deals with Jerusalem alone. Apparently Jeremiah must have said more than is written in the verse, and described the evil somewhat more closely; so that the new matter spoken by him here consists in the "Behold I bring," etc., i.e., in his forewarning them of the speedy fulfilment of the threatenings against Jerusalem and Judah, as was the case with the prophecy in the valley of Benhinnom, which also, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.3">Jer 19:3</reference>, begins with הנני מביא. On "they stiffened their necks," etc., cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.23">Jer 17:23</reference>; Jer 7:26.  <chapter eID="Jer.19"/> <div eID="gen14067" type="x-p"/>

entries.7ce2021e4f68bbfadf2de1f87cacafc311bbe6c4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.19.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.19.1" sID="gen56871" type="section"/> <div sID="gen56872" type="x-p"/>We see that the Prophet was sent by God to shew the people that there was no firmness in that state of which hypocrites boasted; for God, who had favored the people of Israel with singular benefits, did no less retain them in his own possession than the potter. The Prophet had before shewn to the Jews that the potter formed his vessels as he pleased, and also, that when he had taken the clay and the vessel did not please him, he formed another. This prophecy has a similar import, yet it is different, as we shall presently see. The Prophet is here bidden to buy an earthen vessel of the potter, and at the meeting of the people to break it, that all might understand that they were like earthen vessels, and that being thus admonished of their fragility, they might no longer be proud, as though they possessed a firm and perpetual state of happiness.<div eID="gen56872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56873" type="x-p"/>The main object of the two visions is, however, the same: for the Jews thought that they were not subject to the common lot of men, because they had been chosen as a peculiar people; nor would they have gloried in vain with regard to that inestimable privilege, had there been a mutual agreement between God and them; but as they were covenant-breakers, their glorying was vain and foolish, in thinking that God was bound to them. For what right had they to claim this privilege? God indeed had adopted the whole race of Abraham, but there was a condition introduced,<div eID="gen56873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56874" type="x-p"/>“Walk before me and be perfect.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.2">Genesis 17:2</reference>)<div eID="gen56874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56875" type="x-p"/>When they all had become apostates, the covenant, as to them, was abolished. Then God could not have been called, as it were, to an account, as though he had violated his covenant with them, for he owed them nothing. They had become aliens; for through their wickedness and perfidy they had departed from him. God then designed to show how vain and how false was their confidence, when they said, “We are a holy race, we are God’s heritage;” because they had wholly departed from the covenant which God had made with their fathers.<div eID="gen56875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56876" type="x-p"/>But in the form adopted, as I have said, there is some difference. The Prophet had before introduced the potter to shew that there was no less power in God than in a mortal man, because we are before him as the clay, so that he can form and destroy his vessels as he pleases: but here the Prophet shews, that though the Jews had been formed for a time, and so formed as to have been like an excellent and a beautiful vessel, yet it was not a perpetual condition. And it is probable that when they had heard that God could, like the potter, form and re-form them, they had devised an evasion, according to what men usually do who deal sophistically with God, — “O, be it so, the potter can from the same clay form both a precious and a worthless vessel; but we are the precious vessel, and God has given us that form; for when he made a covenant with Abraham, he adorned him with this singular distinction: he afterwards brought our fathers out of Egypt, and then there was a better form added; and since at length he raised a kingdom among us with this promise, that the throne of David would be perpetual, it cannot possibly be otherwise than that we are to continue in our state.” Hence the Prophet expresses here more than in the former prophecy, that not only God had the power of a potter in forming his vessels, but that when the vessel is already formed and possesses great splendor, it can again be broken: he stated this lest the Jews should object by saying, that the state in which they were under David and his posterity would be perpetual. He says, “This is nothing: for the earthen vessel, though splendid and elegant in its form, can yet be broken in the third or fourth year no less than at the time when it is formed, and can be broken for ever,” according to what is afterwards implied by the similitude.<div eID="gen56876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56877" type="x-p"/>We shall proceed now to the words: he says, <hi type="italic">Go and get for thee an earthen vessel</hi>. The Rabbins think the name given to the vessel to be factitious, as the grammarians say, that is, made from its sound; for it appears to have been a flagon or a bottle; and as the bottle has a narrow mouth, it makes this sound, <foreign xml:lang="he">בקבק</foreign> <hi type="italic">bakbuk</hi>, when we drink from it; and hence they think the name is derived. There is, however, no ambiguity as to the thing itself, that the word means a bottle, not only made of earth, but also either of glass or of wood. By adding the word <foreign xml:lang="he">חרש</foreign> <hi type="italic">cheresh</hi>, he specifies what but <foreign xml:lang="he">בקבק</foreign>, <hi type="italic">bekbek</hi>, is a general word. He then adds what is literally, <hi type="italic">From the elders</hi>, and interpreters think that the words “bring with thee” are to be understood; and as to the sense I agree with them, for we shall hereafter see, that in the presence of those who went with him he broke the vessel: it then follows that the elders here spoken of were taken by Jeremiah as his companions; but as <foreign xml:lang="he">מ</foreign> <hi type="italic">mem</hi>, sometimes means “with,” as in the fifty-seventh chapter of Isaiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.57.8">Isaiah 57:8</reference>)<div eID="gen56877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56878" type="x-p"/>“and made thee a covenant with them, <foreign xml:lang="he">מהם</foreign>”<div eID="gen56878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56879" type="x-p"/>I take it to be of the same meaning here; and this is doubtless suitable here, for he was to go <hi type="italic">with the elders of the people and with the elders of the priests</hi> <note n="211"> <div sID="gen56880" type="x-p"/> The literal rendering of this verse I conceive to be the following, —<div eID="gen56880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56881" type="x-p"/>“Thus saith Jehovah, go and get; bottle from the maker of earthenware, and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests.”<div eID="gen56881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56882" type="x-p"/>The <foreign xml:lang="he">מ</foreign>, <hi type="italic">of</hi>, or <hi type="italic">from</hi>, before elders, implies a part; and it is the idiom of the language not to put in “some,” — “get (or take) from the elders,” etc. He was first to get the bottle, and then some of the elders. The <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi> very strangely represents the Prophet as taking the bottle from the elders, omitting the <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign>, and as taking it from both elders! — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen56882" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen56879" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.19.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen56871" osisID="Jer.19.1" type="section"/>
entries.d78fb5f9163aae57effff69112f652c9f19bbb02: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.19.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.19.2" sID="gen56883" type="section"/> <div sID="gen56884" type="x-p"/>And he adds, <hi type="italic">Enter into the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is at the entrance of the east gate</hi>, rendered by some “of the earthen gate,” for which I see no reason; but I leave this to be examined by those who are more versed in the language. It is indeed thought that <foreign xml:lang="he">ש</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shin</hi>, is changed here into <foreign xml:lang="he">ס</foreign>, <hi type="italic">samech</hi>; but if we take the word as it is, it means “solar,” for <foreign xml:lang="he">חרס</foreign> <hi type="italic">cheras</hi>, from which <foreign xml:lang="he">חרסית</foreign> <hi type="italic">cherasit</hi>, is derived, signifies the sun; and it seems to have been called the solar gate by way of excellency, because it looked toward the rising sun. <note n="212"> <div sID="gen56885" type="x-p"/> It appears that the valley of Hinnom was not to the east, but to the south of Jerusalem. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.8">Joshua 15:8</reference>. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> and several copies read <foreign xml:lang="he">החרסית</foreign> and it is given untranslated by the <hi type="italic">Septuagint</hi> the <hi type="italic">Syriac</hi>, and the <hi type="italic">Arabic</hi>. It is rendered “earthen” by the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>, as though the <foreign xml:lang="he">ס</foreign>, as <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi> mentions, is substituted for <foreign xml:lang="he">ש</foreign>. In this case it might be rendered “the potsherd” — “at the entrance of the gate, The potsherd.” It was the gate, before which did lie all the broken vessels, and the dirt and filth from the Temple. For this reason it may be that the <hi type="italic">Targum</hi> renders it here, “the gate of the dunghill.”<div eID="gen56885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56886" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Parkhurst</hi>, however, takes the word as it is in the text, and gives this version, “the gate of the burnings,” so called because of the practice of burning children in the valley opposite the gate. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.31">Jeremiah 7:31</reference>. All these names would properly designate the south gate. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen56886" type="x-p"/> </note> I do not yet oppose the idea of those who think that the Prophet alludes to <foreign xml:lang="he">חרש</foreign>, <hi type="italic">cheresh</hi>, of which he had spoken, and that he calls it the east gate, though it was as it were an earthen gate; for the two letters <foreign xml:lang="he">ש</foreign>, <hi type="italic">shin</hi>, and <foreign xml:lang="he">ס</foreign><hi type="italic"> samech</hi>, as it is well known, are closely allied. <hi type="italic">Cry there</hi>, he says, <hi type="italic">the words which I shall speak to thee.</hi><div eID="gen56884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56887" type="x-p"/>I come now to the subject: God bids his Prophet to get from the potter an earthen vessel, and to do so in the presence of the elders; for it was necessary to have witnesses in a matter so important; and as the public safety of the people was concerned, it was God’s purpose, lest the prophecy should be despised, that there should be present the gravest witnesses, suitable, and, as they say, authorized, or approved; and he calls them the <hi type="italic">elders</hi> of the <hi type="italic">people</hi> and of the <hi type="italic">priests</hi>; and no doubt they were chosen from a great number, even from among the priests who were chief. There were also Levites of the sons of Aaron; but there were then chief priests a large number; but, as they say, it was a turbulent rabble. They were chosen from those first orders who ruled the Church, and Jeremiah calls them the <hi type="italic">elders</hi> of the priests. There were also others chosen from the people who presided over the Church. And we know that there were two public functionaries, or, as they say, a twofold government: the priests were the rulers of the Church with regard to the law, so that their government was spiritual; there were also the elders of the people who managed civil affairs; but there were some things in which they ruled in common. We now then see what the Prophet meant by saying that he was bidden to call witnesses to see what is afterwards stated, and that they were taken partly from the priests and partly from the people.<div eID="gen56887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56888" type="x-p"/>He says; <hi type="italic">Enter into the valley of the son of Hinnom</hi>. This valley was in the suburbs, and was called <foreign xml:lang="he">תפת</foreign> <hi type="italic">Tophet</hi>, as we shall hereafter see. It is thought that this name is derived from drums, because they did beat drums when infants were killed, lest their cry should excite any feeling of humanity. But, we shall again say something on the etymology of this word. In this valley they were accustomed to sacrifice and offer their children by casting them into the fire. Many indeed performed this in a different way, by purifying their children and carrying them round the fire, so that they felt only the flame and escaped unhurt. But there were those who wished to shew their zeal above others, whose ambition drove them farther, and they killed their children and then burnt them. But of this matter I have spoken elsewhere, and I shall now only briefly notice it. This opinion is not, what is commonly received; but it seems to me that it may be gathered from many parts of Scripture, that many killed their children, and that some only purified them. However this may have been, God justly abominated the sacrifice; for his will was that sacrifices should be offered only in one place. When any one offered a calf or a lamb in any other place than at Jerusalem, it was a spurious sacrifice; and the Jews ought to have followed what God had prescribed, and not to have done anything presumptuously, for obedience is ever better than any sacrifices.<div eID="gen56888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56889" type="x-p"/>But here there was a double crime; they left the Temple and sought to obtrude on God sacrifices against his expressed will; and then there was another crime still more atrocious, for they devoted their children to Baalim or to Baal, and not to the only true God. (I pass by now their slaughter and burning.) This then was the reason why the Prophet was commanded to go to this place. How detestable that service was to God appears dear from this, that the prophets give the name of hell to the valley of Hinnom, <foreign xml:lang="he">גיא הנם</foreign> <hi type="italic">gia-enom. </hi>And we know that at the time of Christ it was the common name for hell; and whenever Christ speaks of Gehenna, he uses the word according to its common acceptation at that time. The word has indeed been corrupted by the Greeks, for it is properly <foreign xml:lang="he">גיא הנם</foreign> <hi type="italic">gia-enom</hi>. But what does the word mean in the gospel? Hell itself; and whence was its origin? We indeed know how great and how incurable was the madness of those who gave themselves up to their own superstitions; for though the prophets strongly condemned the place, yet the people proceeded in their usual idolatry; it was therefore necessary to give the place a disgraceful name in order to render it more abominable.<div eID="gen56889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56890" type="x-p"/>It is now added, that the place was <hi type="italic">by the entrance of the east gate</hi>. As it was especially a celebrated gate, and as the sun, rising there, reminded them to behold the light which God had kindled for them in his law, it was a monstrous stupidity proudly to tread, as it were, under foot. the law of God in so renowned a place, and to profane his worship, as though they openly wished to shew that they esteemed as nothing what God had commanded. If any still think that there is an allusion to the word <foreign xml:lang="he">חרש</foreign> <hi type="italic">cheresh</hi>, before used, I offer no opposition; that is, though this gate was indeed oriental, it was yet as it were an earthen gate.<div eID="gen56890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56891" type="x-p"/>He says, <hi type="italic">Cry there,</hi> or, proclaim with a clear voice, <hi type="italic">the words which I shall speak to thee</hi>. The Prophet no doubt said this expressly, in order to add more weight to his prophecy. He indeed did nothing but by God’s command; but as his authority was not acknowledged by the Jews, he here testifies for their sakes that he would say nothing but what God himself would command. This preface then confirmed the authority of his prophecy, so that the Jews might not reject what he might say, as though it came from Jeremiah himself.<div eID="gen56891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56892" type="x-p"/>But a general doctrine may be hence gathered, — that ministers are to bring forward nothing but what they have learnt from God himself. For though Jeremiah was a great man and endued with excellent gifts, yet he was not to bring one word or a syllable as from himself: how great then must be the presumption of those who seek to be superior to him by bringing their inventions, and at the same time demand to be deemed oracles? This passage confirms the doctrine of Peter, who says,<div eID="gen56892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56893" type="x-p"/>“He who speaks, let him speak the words of God.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.4.11">1 Peter 4:11</reference>)<div eID="gen56893" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.19.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen56883" osisID="Jer.19.2" type="section"/>
entries.334d2076d4b80caa4d323215c7ab84a1e8e8ecea:
He now adds, Hear ye the word of Jehovah. This is a confirmation of the former sentence. We hence see why it was said, Cry, or, with a clear voice proclaim, what I shall say to thee; it was, that they might know that he spake not according to his own ideas as a man, but that he was a celestial herald to proclaim what God commanded. Hear, he says, ye kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem. We see how the Prophet did not spare even kings, according to what God had before commanded him, that he should act boldly and shew no respect of persons, (Jeremiah 1:8.) He then faithfully performed his office, as he did not flatter kings, and was not terrified by their dignity and power. But he addressed them first, and then the people, because they who had most grievously sinned, were made rightly to bear the first reproof. We hence see what the next passage means,
“Reprove mountains and chide hills,” (Micah 6:1)
and also this passage,
“I have set thee over nations and kingdoms,” (Jeremiah 1:10)
for heavenly truth ought to bring under subjection, as Paul says, everything high in the world, so that all the pride of man may be subdued. (2 Corinthians 10:5.) Kings indeed do very ill bear to be thus boldly treated; for they wish to be exempt from every law and to be free from every yoke. But if they now acknowledge not their subjection to God’s word, they must at last come before his tribunal; and then they shall find how perversely they have abused their power. As to teachers, they ought, small and great, to teach after the example of Jeremiah; they ought to reprove and to rebuke, when necessary, without shewing any respect of persons.
Thus saith Jehovah of hosts, and the God of Israel, Behold, I am bringing an evil on this place, of which whosoever shall hear, tingle shall his ears. The prophetic word had more power when the Jews were brought to the very place where the event was exhibited, he might have said the same thing in the Temple or in the gate or in the palace of the king but his prophecy would not have been so effectual. We indeed know how much tardiness there is in men in general; but so great was then the obstinacy of the Jews, that however forcibly the truth might have been set forth, yet it was received with so much indifference, that it was neglected. God then intended to shew to them, as it were, the event itself. He says, Jehovah of hosts and the God of Israel; and he used these words, that they might know, as we have stated elsewhere, that they had to do with God, whose power is dreaded even by angels. And in order to shake off their foolish boasting, that they were the children of Abraham, — “God,” he says, “has sufficient power to chastise you, and the same is the God of Israel, whose name ye falsely and absurdly pretend to profess.” These subjects I only in a brief manner handle, because I have explained them more fully elsewhere.
He says that such a calamity was nigh that place as would make the ears to tingle: when there is a violent noise, our ears are stunned, and there is at the same time a certain tingling or ringing. When a man is killed, or when ten or twelve men are slain, there is a dreadful cry; but in a great tumult occasioned by men perishing, such is the noise that it stuns in a manner the ears, like that which proceeds from cataracts; for the violent noise of the Nile, they say, causes some degree of deafness. So also the Prophet says here, I am bringing, says God, a calamity on this place, which shall not only terrify those who will hear of it, but also render them quite astonished, so that their ears shall tingle, as is the case when there is a violent and dreadful noise. The cause follows —
Jeremiah 19:4-5
4. Because they have forsaken me, and have estranged this place, and have burnt incense in it unto other gods, whom neither they nor their fathers have known, nor the kings of Judah, and have filled this place with the blood of innocents;
4. Propterea quod reliquerunt me et alienarunt locum hunc, et suffitum fecerunt in eo diis extraneis, quos non noverunt ipsi neque patres ipsorum, neque reges Jehudah; et implerunt locum hunc sanguine innocentium;
5. They have built also the high places of Baal, to burn their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal, which I commanded not, nor spake it, neither came it into my mind:
5. Et extruxerunt excelsa (aedificarunt excelsa) ipsi Baal, ad comburendum filios suos igne in holocaustum ipsi Baal; quod non mandavi et non loquutus sum, et non ascendit super cor meum (vel, in cot meum.).
entries.a88d2cf26abb90447fa0252c7ae0f9d76fb2fbab: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.19.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.19.4" sID="gen56909" type="section"/> <div sID="gen56910" type="x-p"/>The reason is given why God would so severely deal with that place. We indeed know that hypocrites are ever ready with their answer; as soon as God threatens them, they bark and bring forward their evasions. The Prophet then shews that the judgment announced would be just, lest the Jews should pretend that it was extreme.<div eID="gen56910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56911" type="x-p"/>God first complains that he had been forsaken by them, because they had changed the worship which had been prescribed in his Law. And this is what ought to be carefully considered; for no one would have willingly confessed what Jeremiah charged upon them all; they would have said, — “We have not forsaken God, for we are the children of Abraham; but what we wish to do is to add to his worship; and why should it be deemed a reproach to us, if we are not content with our own simple form of worship, and add various other forms? and we worship God not only in the Temple, but also in this place; and further, we do not spare our own children.” But God shews by one expression that these were frivolous evasions; for he is not acknowledged except what he orders and commands is obediently received. Let us know, that God is forsaken as soon as men turn aside from his pure word, and that all are apostates who turn here and there, and do not follow what God approves.<div eID="gen56911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56912" type="x-p"/>Then he says that they had <hi type="italic">alienated the place</hi>. God had consecrated to himself the whole of Judea: he would not indeed have sacrifices offered to him in every place; but when the Jews worshipped him, as they were taught by Moses and the prophets, the whole land was as it were an altar and a temple to him. Then God complains that his authority in that part of the suburbs was taken away; as though he had said, — “The whole of Judea is my right and my jurisdiction, and Jerusalem is the royal palace in which I dwell; but ye, deluded beings, do by force take away my right and transfer it to another, as though one gave to a robber a place nigh a royal residence.” Thus God justly complains that they had <hi type="italic">alienated</hi> that <hi type="italic">place</hi> <note n="213"> <div sID="gen56913" type="x-p"/> Perhaps the idea would be better expressed, if we were to say, “They had alienized the place,” or heathenized it, made it a heathen place. To alienate is to transfer a right or property from one to another. This was indeed true, for they separated as it were the place from God and transferred it to heathen deities. But the idea here seems to be, that they made the place heathenish: “and have heathenized this place.” “Alienated” is the <hi type="italic">Septuagint</hi>; “made it alien,” the <hi type="italic">Vulgate</hi>; “polluted,” the <hi type="italic">Syriac</hi>; and “defiled,” the <hi type="italic">Targum. </hi>—<hi type="italic"> Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen56913" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen56912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56914" type="x-p"/>But we must remember the reason, which immediately follows, because they had burned incense to Baal. They pretended, no doubt, the name of God; but yet it was a most preposterous superstition, when they worshipped inferior gods, as the Papists do at this day. The word Baal is sometimes used in the singular number by the prophets, and sometimes in the plural: but what is Baal? a patron. They were not content with one patron, but every one desired a patron for himself: hence under the words Baal and Baalim, the prophets characterized all fictition is modes of worship: when they worshipped God’s name, they blended the worship of patrons, who had not been made known to them; hence he adds, <hi type="italic">They have made incense in it to foreign gods</hi>. He afterwards says, that these foreign gods were such as neither they nor their fathers nor their kings knew. By saying that they were gods unknown to their fathers as well as to themselves and to their kings, he no doubt calls their attention to the doctrine of the law, and to the many certain proofs by which they had found that he was the only true God.<div eID="gen56914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56915" type="x-p"/>The Jews might have raised such an objection as the Papists do at this day, — that their modes of worship were not devised in their time, but that they had derived them from their ancestors. But God regarded as nothing those kings and the fathers, who had long before degenerated from true and genuine religion. It must be here observed, that true knowledge is connected with verity: for they who had first contrived new forms of worship, doubtless followed their own foolish imaginations; as when any one in the present day asks the Papists, why they weary themselves so much with their superstitions, good intention is ever their shield, — “O, we think that this is pleasing to God.” Therefore rightly does God here repudiate their inventions as wholly vain, for they possess nothing solid or permanent. At the same time, he by implication condemns the Jews for rejecting his law, whose authority had been established among them, so that they ought not to have entertained any doubt: for it would have been the greatest ingratitude to say, “We know not who introduced the Law!” God had indeed sanctioned the law by so many miracles, that it could not have been disputed; and they had also found by many evidences and proofs that he was the only brue God. tie had then been known by their fathers as well as by their kings, even by David and by all his godly successors.
